content: When an individual receives a positive HIV diagnosis in community settings, such as through mobile health services, community centers, or home-based testing, they are typically referred to a health facility to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART). The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends starting ART as quickly as possible, ideally on the same day as the diagnosis, to address the significant drop-off observed between diagnosis and treatment initiation. However, ensuring rapid ART initiation across diverse settings and populations remains a challenge. A systematic review conducted in 2018 in sub-Saharan Africa revealed that linkage to care after community-based HIV testing was alarmingly low, with only 14% of individuals linked to care after home-based testing and 10% after community-based testing. In some cases, fewer than 25% of individuals had started treatment. Common reasons for not initiating treatment included feeling healthy, lack of social support, stigma, high costs of seeking care, and incomplete understanding of the benefits of treatment. These barriers are particularly concerning for vulnerable populations, such as women, young girls, and key populations, who face heightened risks of stigma, discrimination, and violence. Early initiation of ART is associated with numerous health benefits, including reduced mortality and morbidity and decreased onward transmission of HIV. Offering ART initiation before referral to a health facility can reduce delays for individuals who are unwilling or unable to attend a facility. Studies assessing community-based ART initiation have not reported intervention-specific harms but emphasize the importance of providing baseline assessments and support, either as part of the intervention or upon referral to a health facility. When ART initiation is integrated into existing community activities, additional expertise and resources are required. For example, a randomized trial in South Africa and Uganda estimated the annual per-client cost of community-based ART initiation to be between $275 and $452, slightly higher than the $214 to $422 cost for facility-based initiation. Another study in Malawi found that home-based ART initiation following HIV self-testing cost an average of $172 per participant annually, compared to $858 to $1,165 for facility-based ART provision. Implementing community-based ART initiation can improve access to treatment for individuals facing structural barriers, such as criminalization, stigma, and discrimination. For instance, a study among female sex workers in Tanzania found that those receiving community-based ART initiation were more likely to start treatment, remain in care, and experience lower levels of internalized stigma. However, evidence for adolescents is limited, and the acceptability of such approaches remains uncertain. WHO guidelines recommend readiness assessments at the time of ART initiation, including ART literacy and clinical evaluations, such as CD4 cell counts, to identify advanced HIV disease and determine the need for further diagnostics and prophylaxis. Nurses should be empowered to initiate ART, supported by professional regulations. Clients starting ART outside health facilities should be linked to long-term care models and provided with counseling to ensure lifelong adherence. For those not ready to start ART, referral to care should be facilitated. ART initiation outside health facilities must include appropriate risk assessments and counseling support, both at the time of initiation and afterward. This recommendation applies to all people living with HIV, including children and adolescents. However, there is limited experience with ART initiation outside facilities for infants and young children, and antiretroviral drug formulations for these age groups may require additional guidance on administration techniques and storage conditions. Community health-care providers should be trained and equipped to deliver effective counseling to caregivers and support appropriate drug administration. Adolescents should be linked to psychosocial care, and children and parents should receive support for disclosure and age-appropriate treatment literacy within a family-based care approach. Implementing community-based ART initiation requires adaptations to health systems, including ensuring drug supply chains, laboratory services, training and supervision of health personnel, preventive therapy, and referral mechanisms for higher-level care. A phased approach may be necessary, starting in settings where community prevention and testing activities are already established. Community HIV care should be integrated into national initiatives to ensure quality care. Research is needed to better understand client preferences regarding ART initiation locations and linkage to care by age, population, and setting. Tools to support ART initiation outside health facilities should be designed and evaluated. Evidence shows variability in the size and composition of community treatment teams, and implementation research could help define optimal staffing and skill requirements. Additionally, research on how ART initiation outside facilities affects household spending and catastrophic costs would be valuable. Rapid ART initiation, including same-day start, should be offered to all individuals living with HIV following a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment. Rapid initiation is defined as starting ART within seven days of diagnosis, with priority given to individuals with advanced HIV disease. Same-day ART initiation should be offered to those ready to start, accompanied by tailored patient education, counseling, and support to improve uptake, adherence, and retention. In 2017, WHO strongly recommended rapid ART initiation for all people living with HIV, supported by evidence showing increased likelihood of treatment initiation, improved viral load suppression, and better retention in care. However, uptake of this recommendation in national policies has been variable. Some studies have reported poorer retention in care with same-day ART initiation compared to less rapid initiation, highlighting the importance of good counseling and respectful, non-judgmental health personnel. A systematic review identified 26 studies examining strategies to accelerate ART initiation, including interventions targeting clients, health-care providers, and health systems. These strategies were associated with increased ART uptake, viral load suppression at 12 months, and retention in care. The WHO Guideline Development Group emphasized the importance of implementing additional strategies to facilitate same-day ART uptake and improve outcomes. Evidence-informed approaches to support same-day ART initiation include reducing administrative and psychosocial requirements, providing first ART counseling on the day of HIV testing, and offering decision support tools. Post-initiation strategies, such as appointment reminders and intensified counseling, can further improve outcomes. For individuals established on ART, clinical visits and ART refills every 3–6 months are recommended, with six-month intervals preferred if feasible. This approach reduces patient travel costs, time spent accessing care, and health system costs, making it a cost-saving intervention. Reducing the frequency of drug dispensing requires adequate drug supply and appropriate storage options for clients, including for community ART delivery. Providing less frequent health service interactions can improve equity by increasing access to care for vulnerable and mobile populations.
